source_text: Et haec quidem quantum spectat ad testimonium Apostoli disputata sunt. Ceterum in Isaia, unde ipsam sententiam Paulus assumpsit, in tantum non deterret Deus rationabilem creaturam a sui consideratione iudicii, ut sicut per eumdem Prophetam dixerat: Quiescite agere perverse, discite bene facere, subvenite oppresso; et venite, arguite me, dicit Dominus [n368] ; ita etiam hic, ne quid potestate sola, non iustitia videretur fecisse, dispensationum suarum dignatur aperire rationem. Afflicto enim in captivitate populo Iudaeorum redemptionis appropiare tempus, quo ad terram suam reverterentur, annuntiat; et causam vel praecedentium angorum reserat, vel instantium gaudiorum. Epuletur, inquit, caelum desuper, et nubes spargant iustitiam; oriatur ex terra misericordia, et iustitia oriatur simul. Ego sum Dominus Deus qui creavi te, faciens meliorem, praeparavi te sicut lutum figuli. Numquid qui arat, arabit terram per omnem diem? Numquid dicit lutum figulo: Quid facis, quia non operaris, quia non habes manus? Numquid dicit figmentum ei qui se finxit: Sapienter me finxisti? Vel qui dicit patri: Quid generabis? Et matri: Quid parturies? Quia sic dicit Dominus Deus Israel sanctus, qui fecit futura: Interrogate me pro filiis meis et filiabus, et pro operibus manuum mearum mandate mihi. Ego feci terram et hominem super eam; ego manu mea firmavi caelum; ego omnibus sideribus mandavi; ego levavi cum iustitia regem, et omnes viae eius rectae; hic aedificabit civitatem meam, et captivitatem populi mei reducet, non cum praemio, nec cum muneribus, dixit Dominus Sabaoth [n369] .
pass_a_gloss: And these things indeed as much as looks to the testimony of the Apostle have been disputed. For the rest in Isaiah, from where Paul took up the sentence itself, God so far does not deter a rational creature from the consideration of his judgment, that as through the same Prophet he had said: Cease to act perversely, learn to do well, come under to the oppressed; and come, argue me, says the Lord; so also here, lest he seem to have done anything by power alone, not by justice, he deigns to open the reason of his dispensations. For to the people of the Jews afflicted in captivity he announces the time of redemption to approach, by which they would be returned to their own land; and he unbars the cause either of preceding distresses, or of joys standing near. Let heaven feast, he says, from above, and let the clouds scatter justice; let mercy arise from the earth, and let justice arise together. I am the Lord God who created you, making better, I have prepared you as clay of a potter. Will he who plows, plow the land through every day? Does the clay say to the potter: What are you doing, because you are not working, because you have not hands? Does the thing fashioned say to him who fashioned it: Have you fashioned me wisely? Or who says to a father: What will you generate? And to a mother: What will you bring forth? Because thus says the Lord God the holy of Israel, who made future things: Ask me for my sons and daughters, and for the works of my hands mandate me. I made the earth and the human upon it; I by my hand firmed heaven; I commanded all the stars; I have lifted a king with justice, and all his ways are straight; this one will build my city, and will lead back the captivity of my people, not with a prize, nor with gifts, said the Lord of Hosts.

lemmas.lexica: LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: These arguments concern the apostle's testimony. In Isaiah, however, from whom Paul took the statement itself, God is so far from deterring rational creatures from examining his judgment that he deigns to explain the reasoning of his dealings, lest he seem to have acted by power alone rather than justice. Through the same prophet he had said: “Cease acting perversely, learn to do good, help the oppressed; and come, argue with me, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:16–18) (Isaiah 29:16). Here likewise he announces to the Jewish people suffering in captivity that the time of redemption is approaching, when they will return to their own land. He discloses the reason both for their preceding distress and for their coming joy.

He says: “Let heaven above feast, and let the clouds scatter righteousness; let mercy arise from the earth, and let righteousness arise together with it. I am the Lord God who created you; making you better, I prepared you like a potter's clay. Will the plowman plow the earth all day? (Isaiah 28:24) Does the clay say to the potter, ‘What are you doing? You are not working; you have no hands’? Does what is molded say to the one who molded it, ‘Did you mold me wisely?’ (compare Isaiah 29:16) Or does someone say to a father, ‘What will you beget?’ and to a mother, ‘What will you give birth to?’ For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who made the things to come: ‘Question me about my sons and daughters, and give me instructions about the works of my hands. I made the earth and the human being upon it; with my own hand I established heaven; I commanded all the stars. I have raised up a king with righteousness, and all his ways are straight. He will build my city and bring back my people's captivity, not for a reward or for gifts,’ says the Lord of Hosts” (Isaiah 45:8–13, LXX-based wording).

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.

variants.reading: This quotation preserves Julian’s composite Old Latin wording rather than replacing it with a modern Bible. The source identifies Isaiah 45:8–13, but the plowman question also quotes Isaiah 28:24, and the question about the maker’s wisdom recalls Isaiah 29:16.
